newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ANALYSTS AWAIT STRATEGY NEWS FROM PHILIPS.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS AWAIT STRATEGY NEWS FROM PHILIPS.

text.p: A promise of aggressive restructuring at Philips from new chairman Cor Boonstra on Thursday drew support from markets but Philips watchers said on Friday they need to know how he is going to handle strategy.

Markets have greeted Boonstra's tough talking at Thursday's third quarter results news conference with a surge of buying for Philips shares, driving up the shares 4.50 guilders higher to 61.10 guilders over two days.
But questions remain unanswered as to how Boonstra will rebuild profits after he has tackled Philips' cost base.
Susan Anthony of Schroders in London welcomed Boonstra's remarks about cost cutting and weeding out nonperforming businesses, either by closing them or selling them.

"But I still feel that in the absence of hearing from him his strategy for Philips, where he sees this company going over the next three or four years, I think we're being asked to take a lot on face value to believe he's going to succeed," she said.

Philips, Europe's largest consumer electronics firm, on Thursday said it expected a one billion guilder restructuring charge in the fourth quarter, on top of an 800 million gross second quarter charge to reorganise its Sound & Vision unit.

Analysts, totting up the charges from Philips' Centurion recovery plan in the early 1990s, point out that by the end of 1996 the company will have put aside something approaching six billion guilders for restructuring during the decade.

"What we want to know is whether this wipes the slate clean or whether we can continue to expect them to take what has amounted to a billion guilder charge every year," said another analyst, who declined to be named.
"The main question comes back, is this something that has to happen every two years or the beginning of a new era? I think it's somewhere in between," said ING analyst Eric de Graaf.
Anthony said Boonstra's predecessor Jan Timmer had achieved a huge amount in cost cutting, but said the group needed to be reshaped so it could achieve sustainable profit growth.
"So far it's been able to improve in the wake of big restructuring charges but then something happens and it all goes horribly wrong," she said.

Philips on Thursday stunned investors with a 77 percent slump in net profit from normal operations to 123 million guilders -- half the lowest forecast from analysts -- and drew admissions from Boonstra that the company had disappointed for the past four or five quarters.

Analysts say this year's profit performance from Philips is now of academic interest with expectations that the firm could finish 1996 narrowly either side of break-even at the bottom line compared to 1995's net profit of 2.5 billion guilders.
"Hard figures are not that important right now it's more the story of strong actions and the effects they will have on profitability," said ING's De Graaf.

"If Philips is going to take another billion (charge) in the fourth quarter then the only way is up after that. Next year is a recovery year because of the low base year this year, the real recovery of markets we don't expect before 1998," he said.
Schroders' Anthony is looking for a 1997 net profit of 1.975 billion guilders and is retaining her estimate of 2.95 billion for net profit in 1998.
"You can't call that miraculous because that's taking them back to not much greater than they were in 1995, so I don't think we should get carried away there.

"I'd like to think in February with the full year results that Mr Boonstra would have something broadly to say. I think I'd like to hear something by then. This is a company which has got to change from being too slow in response to changes, we need to see that message coming from the top," she said. -- Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
